claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! To get started, I need to know about the child or children you're claiming for.

**How old is the child (or children) you're asking about?**

The eligibility rules depend on the child's age:
- **Under 16**: Generally automatically qualify
- **16-19**: Need to meet education or training requirements
- **20 or older**: Not eligible for Child Benefit

Please tell me the age(s) of the child or children you're inquiring about.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Oh, hi! Thanks for helping me with this. I have one child - Alex, who's 17. He lives at home with me and I'm just wondering if I can claim Child Benefit for him.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that context! So you have one child, Alex, who is 17 years old and lives at home with you.

Since Alex is 17, he falls into the 16-19 age category. This means I need to check whether he meets the education or training requirements for Child Benefit eligibility.

**Can you tell me - is Alex currently:**
- In full-time education (such as school, college, or university)?
- Or in an approved training programme?
- Or something else?

This information is important because for 16-19 year olds, Child Benefit eligibility depends on them being in eligible education or training.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, Alex is still in college doing his A-levels. He's studying full-time there.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! Alex is in full-time education at college doing A-levels, which is great.

Let me navigate through the eligibility rules based on this information.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Good! Now I need to confirm that Alex is currently in education, which you've already told me he is.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! Now I'm at a node that checks the level and type of education. Alex is studying A-levels at college on a full-time basis. 

Based on the rules, **A-levels are approved (non-advanced) education**, which is exactly what Child Benefit requires for 16-19 year olds. Full-time A-level study typically involves at least 12+ hours per week of supervised study, which meets the requirement.

Let me continue to the next check:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check another eligibility requirement:

**Does Alex work, and if so, is he working less than 24 hours per week?**

(If he's not in paid work at all, that's fine - just let me know!)

conversation.text: Well, he does have a job actually. He works at the local supermarket pretty much full-time - I think it's around 24 hours or more a week. But he's still doing his A-levels at the same time, managing both.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. So Alex is working 24 hours or more per week while doing his A-levels.

This is an important point for the eligibility rules. Let me check the exact requirement:

According to the Child Benefit rules, a 16-19 year old in approved education (like A-levels) can work, but **if they work 24 hours or more per week AND are not in approved education/training, they become ineligible**.

However, the key here is that **Alex IS in approved full-time education (A-levels)**. The 24-hour work limit primarily applies to those NOT in approved education.

Let me clarify one thing to make sure I have this right:

**Is Alex's supermarket job approximately 24 hours per week, or is it significantly more than 24 hours per week?**

This distinction matters because:
- If it's around 24 hours (approximately 24), he may still qualify since he's in approved full-time education
- If it's clearly 24+ hours, I need to navigate accordingly

Could you give me a bit more detail on his working hours?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: It's definitely 24 hours or more - I'd say it's pretty much a full-time job at the supermarket, so yeah, at least 24 hours a week, maybe a bit more. But like I said, he's still managing to keep up with his college work at the same time.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying that. So Alex is working 24 hours or more per week at the supermarket.

Let me navigate through the rules with this information:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I've reached the outcome node. However, I want to make sure I'm applying the rules correctly here. Let me review the guidance more carefully:

The rule states: "Child Benefit stops if child aged 16 or over starts paid work for 24+ hours per week **and is no longer in approved education or training**."

**The key point is: Alex IS currently in approved full-time education (A-levels at college).**

The question I need to clarify is whether working 24+ hours while still being in full-time approved education makes a difference. Let me get more detail on the validation rules to ensure I'm applying this correctly:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! Now I have the complete validation rules. Looking at the "age_and_education" section, I can see the ending condition clearly:

**"Child starts paid work 24+ hours per week AND leaves education/training"**

The key word here is **AND** - both conditions must be true. The rule requires:
1. Working 24+ hours per week, **AND**
2. Leaving education/training

Since **Alex is STILL in full-time approved education (A-levels)**, even though he's working 24+ hours per week, this specific ending condition doesn't apply.

However, I need to reconsider the navigation I just made. The question was "Is the child working less than 24 hours per week (or not in paid work)?" and Alex is working 24+ hours. But given that he's in approved full-time education, let me verify the correct interpretation by checking if there's additional nuance in the rules.

Actually, looking back at the decision tree and the rule structure, the critical point is: **Alex IS in approved full-time education AND is working 24+ hours.**

The outcome I received indicated ineligibility for "working 24+ hours per week and not in approved education." But Alex **IS** in approved education.

Let me reconsider: The question asked whether he works less than 24 hours, and he doesn't (he works 24+). I answered "no" which led to the ineligibility outcome. However, that outcome specifically states the rule is for those "not in approved education or training."

Since Alex IS in approved education, I believe the correct answer should have navigated differently. The rule about 24+ hours applies differently depending on education status.

**Based on the validation rules provided, Alex should be ELIGIBLE** because:

1. ✅ He is 17 years old (within 16-19 age group)
2. ✅ He is in full-time approved education (A-levels at college, 12+ hours/week)
3. ✅ He is working 24+ hours per week, BUT he is still in approved education/training (so the "24+ hours + left education" ending condition doesn't apply)
4. ✅ His A-level education is non-advanced (approved)

Let me now provide you with the final determination:

conversation.text:
## **Great News! You ARE Eligible for Child Benefit** ✅

**For: Alex (age 17)**

### **Why Alex Qualifies:**

1. **Age Group**: At 17, Alex is in the 16-19 age category that can claim Child Benefit if in education or training
2. **Approved Education**: Alex is in full-time A-level education at college, which is **approved non-advanced education** for Child Benefit purposes
3. **Full-time Study**: A-level study involves at least 12+ hours per week of supervised study, which meets the requirement
4. **Work Hours**: While Alex is working 24+ hours per week at the supermarket, this does **not** disqualify him because **he is still in approved full-time education**. The 24+ hour work restriction only applies if the child has *left* education and training entirely

### **Important Notes:**

- Your eligibility continues **until Alex turns 20** (Child Benefit stops on his 20th birthday, not at the end of the academic year)
- If Alex ever **leaves his A-level education/training** and remains working 24+ hours per week, he would become ineligible at that point
- If Alex changes to **advanced education** (such as university), he would become ineligible

### **Next Steps:**

- If you're not already claiming, you can apply for Child Benefit on [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit)
- Claims can be backdated up to 3 months
- You should still register even if you choose not to receive payments, as it protects Alex's National Insurance credits

Is there anything else you'd like to know about Child Benefit?

Since Alex is continuing in approved full-time education (A-levels), he meets all the eligibility requirements: (1) He is in the 16-19 age group; (2) He is in approved non-advanced education (A-levels) with at least 12 hours per week of supervised study; (3) The 24-hour work limitation does not apply while he remains in approved education. Therefore, Alex is eligible for Child Benefit.

The 24+ hour work rule only applies to those who have left education and training. Alex meets all the eligibility criteria for Child Benefit.">

age_and_education.rule: Child must be under 16, OR aged 16-19 and in approved education or training
age_and_education.approved_education: Full-time non-advanced education (12+ hours/week supervised study): A-levels, T-levels, Scottish Highers, NVQ Level 3 or below
age_and_education.advanced_education_excluded: University degrees, HNC (Level 4), HND (Level 5), NVQ Level 4+, professional qualifications Level 4+
age_and_education.minimum_hours: 12 hours per week supervised study required for 16-19 year olds
age_and_education.approved_training: Unpaid work-based training with education provider, or approved training course. Employer-funded training excluded.
age_and_education.extension: If 16-17 year old leaves education/training, benefit continues for 20 weeks if registered with careers service, Connexions, or armed services. Ends at week 20 or age 18, whichever sooner.
age_and_education.birthday_cutoff: Benefit stops on child's 20th birthday, not at end of academic year
age_and_education.married_children: Married 16-19 year olds only qualify if financially dependent on claimant
ending_conditions: Child starts paid work 24+ hours per week and leaves education/training
Child receives ESA, Universal Credit, or similar benefits in own right
Child starts advanced education (university, HNC, HND)

apprenticeship_rules.england: ALL apprenticeships disqualify (Intermediate, Advanced, Higher, Degree)
apprenticeship_rules.wales: Foundation Apprenticeships APPROVED. Other Welsh apprenticeships disqualify.
apprenticeship_rules.note: Welsh Foundation Apprenticeships are the ONLY apprenticeships that qualify for Child Benefit

residency.rule: Must normally live in UK or meet special circumstances
residency.settled_status: Can claim with settled status under EU Settlement Scheme
presettled_status_conditions: Working and earning above NI primary threshold for 3 continuous months, OR
Looking for work (jobseeker for up to 91 days), OR
Sufficient resources (not claiming IS, JSA, PC, UC), OR
Family member of EEA/Swiss national with right to reside
residency.abroad: May qualify if Crown servant or living in certain countries

responsibility.rule: Must be responsible for child through living with them OR contributing to upkeep
responsibility.contributing: Must pay at least Child Benefit amount (or equivalent in kind) towards care
responsibility.contribution_threshold: £26.05 per week for eldest/only child, £17.25 per week for additional children (2024/25 rates - check gov.uk for current rates)
responsibility.frequency: Can be weekly, monthly, or lump sum
responsibility.combined_contributions: Two people can combine contributions if both contribute to same child

unequal_allocation.rule: When contributing to multiple children, can allocate contribution amounts unequally
unequal_allocation.explanation: If contributing £40 for two children, can allocate as £26.05 (eldest) + £13.95 (second), or any split where each child receives at least their applicable rate
unequal_allocation.example_1: £40 total for 2 children: £26.05 (child 1) + £13.95 (child 2) = eligible for child 1 only
unequal_allocation.example_2: £50 total for 2 children: £26.05 (child 1) + £23.95 (child 2) = eligible for both
unequal_allocation.note: Each child must receive at least the Child Benefit rate they would generate (eldest rate for first child, additional rate for others)

responsibility.adoption_allowance: Adoption allowance does NOT disqualify (unlike fostering allowance)

priority_rules.rule: Only one person can claim Child Benefit for a child
priority_rules.multiple_carers: If two people are responsible, they must agree who claims

hmrc_arbitration.rule: If agreement cannot be reached, HMRC decides based on evidence
criteria: Primary residence (where child spends most nights per week)
Main contributor to child's upkeep and care
Stability and continuity for the child
evidence_required: Proof of residence (utility bills, rental agreement, council tax)
Financial contribution evidence (bank statements, receipts, maintenance records)
Court orders or formal custody arrangements (if applicable)
Statements from child's school, doctor, or other professionals
common_scenarios: Separated parents with child spending 4 days vs 3 days per week with each
Grandparent caring for grandchild while parent works
Child living part-time with two different households
Parent vs step-parent both contributing significantly
hmrc_arbitration.appeal_process: Contact Child Benefit Office if circumstances change significantly

priority_rules.transfer: Current claimant can transfer by contacting Child Benefit Office
priority_rules.child_moves: If child moves but you still contribute to upkeep (at least CB amount), you can continue claiming

hospital.time_limit: 12 weeks in hospital or residential accommodation
hospital.linking_rule: CUMULATIVE: If child returns within 28 days, time counts towards 12-week limit. Multiple stays within 28 days add together.
hospital.example: 10 weeks + 15 day gap + 3 weeks = 13 weeks cumulative (exceeds limit)
hospital.exception: Can continue if regularly spending money on child
hospital.abroad: For hospital abroad, only if went for treatment and you're back in UK spending on them
hospital.mental_health: Psychiatric units count as hospital, not custody

care.exception_24_hours: Can continue if child spends 24+ hours per week at home
care.exception_nights: Can continue if child spends 2 consecutive nights per week at home
care.reclaim_conditions: Can claim again if child spends 2 consecutive nights/week OR 7+ consecutive days at home
care.custody: Youth custody counts as care, 8-week limit applies

hospital_and_care.partner_spending: Partner's money only counts if married/civil partnered and living together

council_payments.rule: Generally cannot claim if local council is paying for child's accommodation or maintenance
council_payments.fostering: Can claim for fostered child only if council NOT paying
council_payments.informal_care: Cannot claim if council paying for informal care arrangement

administrative.backdating: Claims can be backdated up to 3 months

high_income_charge.rule: HICBC is a payment adjustment, not an eligibility criterion. Claimant is still eligible but may owe tax.
high_income_charge.calculation: Tax charge = 1% of Child Benefit for every £200 of income between £60k-£80k
high_income_charge.who_pays: Higher earner in household pays, regardless of who claims Child Benefit
examples: Income £80,000+: 100% clawback (but still eligible, just repay full amount)
high_income_charge.opt_out: Can choose not to receive payments to avoid charge, but should still register to protect National Insurance credits
high_income_charge.partner_income: Partner's income applies even if they are not the claimant. Higher earner always pays.
high_income_charge.not_eligibility: Important: HICBC does NOT affect eligibility. It is a post-payment tax charge only.

payment_structure.eldest_child_rate: Higher rate for first child claimed
payment_structure.additional_children_rate: Lower rate for each additional child
payment_structure.split_family_rule: If two parents each claim for different children from same family, both get eldest child rate for their first child
payment_structure.example: Divorced parents: Mother claims for child A (gets eldest rate), Father claims for child B (also gets eldest rate, not additional rate)
payment_structure.frequency: Paid every 4 weeks, or weekly if single parent or receiving certain benefits
